newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian president recalls ideals on historic day.
newsitem.headline: Romanian president recalls ideals on historic day.

text.p: Reformist President Emil Constantinescu called on Romanians on Sunday, two days after taking office, to honour the ideals of their ancestors by fighting poverty and moving closer to the rest of Europe.

Constantinescu marked the 78th anniversary of the unification of Romanian lands at the end of World War One with a pledge to fulfil his election promises of improving living standards which tumbled under his ex-communist predecessor.

But his address to 20,000 people who braved drizzle outside the cathedral where Transylvania was declared reunited with Romania on December 1, 1918 was less dramatic than fiery campaign speeches and an address in taking the oath in office.

"I call on you to stand against poverty, corruption and despondency. I know that many of you are poor, have been betrayed in your expectations and are disoriented by a new society," Constantinescu said.
"I know that I am the incarnation of your hopes for the better along with the government to emerge in a few days. Romania cannot allow these hopes to go unfulfilled."
Romanians wanting to be part of the European fold, he said, had to return to the traditional values of previous generations -- church, family, school and the army.

Constantinescu won last month's presidential election by defeating Ion Iliescu, a former aide to Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu who took power in the aftermath of the violent 1989 revolt in which Ceausescu was toppled and shot.
He campaigned on pledges to bridge the growing economic gap with ex-communist countries which pursued faster reforms -- like Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland.

His centrist Democratic Convention, which also ousted ex-communists in general elections last month, is committed to a combination of budget discipline and improved benefits to the elderly and other groups worst hit by economic transition.

Constantinescu leaves later on Sunday for Portugal to tell a summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe that Romania views membership of NATO and the European Union as its top foreign policy objectives.
The ceremonies in Alba Iulia were the focus of nationwide festivities marking Romania's national day on December 1.

Constantinescu's visit to the city in the heart of Transylvania crowned his formal swearing-in on Friday in the opulent palace erected by Ceausescu -- Bucharest's most tangible symbol of the late dictator's megalomania.
Earlier on Sunday he joined worshippers for a religious service led by Orthodox Church leaders in the main cathedral in the city, 400 km (250 miles) northwest of Bucharest.
Athletes representing the country's various regions paraded before the crowd cheering "Emil, Emil," outside the cathedral.

Constantinescu told the crowd, including peasants in traditional black sheepskin hats, that the reunification of 1918 was "the triumph of a dream, the most beautiful dream of our entire history. Romanians got back their borders, national identity and strength."
The euphoria of the 100,000 Romanians who witnessed the 1918 proclamation restoring Transylvania was shortlived.
In 1940, Romania lost the territories of northern Bucovina and southern Bessarabia to the Soviet Union under secret protocols of the Nazi-Soviet pact.
The lands remain to this day in the former Soviet republics of Ukraine and Moldova, where links with Romania were an issue in a presidential runoff held on Sunday.
A handful of placards in Alba Iulia called for the recreation of Greater Romania, but such sentiment is generally confined to a few fringe parties.
